title: We are at this once again.
text: We are at this once again. Public Health is also Global Health. The Ebola epidemic that is raging in Congo (Mongbwalu district in the east) in the gold mining district is heart-wrenching. Ok, let me "mog" or go "AMOG" on any readers who will stick with me:The specific strain is Bundibugyo virus, one of the Ebola viruses. It is not Zaire ebolavirus, which matters because the licensed Ebola vaccine and monoclonal treatments are mainly for Zaire, not Bundibugyo. WHO says there is no licensed vaccine or specific approved therapeutic yet for Bundibugyo disease, though candidates are being evaluated.Transmission: same Ebola pattern: direct contact with blood/body fluids of a symptomatic infected person, contaminated needles/surfaces, unsafe burial practices, and infected animals. It is not airborne like measles/COVID. Incubation is generally 2â21 days; people are not considered contagious before symptoms. CDC lists current symptoms as fever, body pain, weakness, vomiting, and sometimes bleeding.Survival / fatality: current confirmed-case CFR is still unstable because many suspected cases are not fully classified. WHO reported 125 confirmed cases and 17 deaths as of May 27, 2026, about 14% among confirmed cases, but also 906 suspected cases with 223 suspected deaths. WHO notes past Bundibugyo outbreaks had CFRs around 30â50%.So, the practical read is less well-covered by existing Ebola countermeasures than Zaire Ebola, potentially 30â50% fatal historically, but current confirmed CFR may be artificially low/early due to reporting lag and case classification.In the coming days, weeks, and months we will know a lot more and efforts will be made to develop a vaccine. However, the global politics AND the US role in it are frankly, shameful. This is who we really are, our current actions, budgetary priorities, and rhetoric from our leaders reflect our values.The current U.S. administration’s position appears to be a combination of limited overseas Ebola-response support, aggressive border-control measures, and a strong emphasis on protecting Americans rather than leading a large international containment effort. That is a noticeable shift from the 2014â2016 Ebola response, when the U.S. played a much larger global leadership role.What the U.S. is doingThe administration has:Activated a CDC emergency response and increased airport screening of travelers arriving from affected regions.Imposed travel restrictions on people coming from affected countries, including temporary restrictions affecting some green-card holders who recently traveled to the Democratic Republic of Congo, Uganda, or South Sudan.Provided emergency funding (about $23 million initially) to support Ebola response efforts in the affected countries.Funded deployment of Ebola treatment units and coordinated CDC personnel and supplies.Explored experimental monoclonal antibody therapies and treatment options.What has changed from prior Ebola outbreaksSeveral major changes have occurred:The U.S. withdrew from the World Health Organization, reducing direct coordination through WHO mechanisms.USAID's former global outbreak-response infrastructure has largely been dismantled or reorganized.Foreign aid and global health-security funding have been reduced compared with previous years.Critics argue these changes have weakened international containment efforts and contributed to slower responses on the ground."Only U.S. citizens?" — what appears to be the current stanceThe administration's public messaging has focused heavily on preventing Ebola from entering the United States.Secretary of State Marco Rubio stated that the U.S. "cannot allow any Ebola cases" to enter the country. Current policy discussions have emphasized:screening and travel restrictions,quarantine planning for Americans exposed overseas,and treatment of infected Americans outside the U.S. when feasible.One striking example involved an American physician who contracted Ebola in Congo and was evacuated to Germany rather than the United States, reportedly after internal debate within the administration.The practical message seems to be:Protect Americans first, reduce importation risk, provide some international assistance, but avoid the kind of large-scale U.S.-led global Ebola intervention seen in 2014.Is the response adequate?That depends on the perspective.Administration supporters argue:The immediate risk to the U.S. public remains low.Border screening and travel controls are appropriate.Resources should be focused on protecting Americans.Many infectious-disease experts argue:Ebola is best stopped at its source.Cuts to global-health programs, CDC capacity, USAID networks, and WHO cooperation have reduced the world's ability to contain outbreaks early.Investing overseas is often cheaper and safer than dealing with imported cases later.As of late May 2026, the outbreak in the Democratic Republic of Congo and Uganda is still expanding, with WHO describing it as outpacing current response efforts.

title: This is a very interesting anecdote in the WSJ about a newer, little understood therapy for…
text:
This is a very interesting anecdote in the WSJ about a newer, little understood therapy for severe depression (EMDR)! 

It is no secret that mental health and illness are challenges that are highly prevalent in both children and adults, especially depression and crippling anxiety. The causes are complex, likely some combination of childhood trauma/experiences, brain chemistry, genetics, and perhaps environmental or dietary triggers.  The standard approach involves a motivated person who voluntarily seeks out care from a professional, which includes some form of behavioral or talk therapy and a medication (most often an anti-depressant).

There are major advances that are happening in mental health circles that are changing the standard paradigm.  Biological theories are evolving beyond serotonin, and a major intellectual shift is occurring. The older “chemical imbalance” serotonin narrative is now considered oversimplified.

Navigating the healthcare (and insurance maze) is immensely difficult for mental illness even with an intact support structure, and I would say more so than obvious physical illness.  

Rapid-acting antidepressants: ketamine and esketamine (Spravato)

This is probably the biggest paradigm shift in modern depression treatment.  Many patients describe “mental relief”, reduced suicidal intensity, emotional opening less rigid thinking within 24 hours. FDA approved in 2019, then in 2025 as monotherapy for "treatment-resistant depression."  Mechanism of action is quite different (not on basis of serotonin, dopamine, or norepinephrine) and is based on a novel glutamate NMDA receptor antagonism that causes downstream effects, instead of slowly nudging serotonin levels, ketamine/esketamine may rapidly “re-open” neural flexibility and connectivity.

Intranasal esketamine (Spravato) made by J&J: Esketamine is the FDA-approved S-enantiomer of ketamine. This requires 2-hour observed therapy sessions in a REMS-clinic 2X/wk. initially for 4 weeks (with dose titration), then once per week for 4 weeks, then maintenance every 1-2 weeks, does not require anesthesia, patient cannot drive for 24 hours; it is currently expensive and insurers may cover some of the cost; Esketamine formulation itself is new so the price is high, out of pocket was quoted to me as $1500-2000 per session (presumably includes the observation time), which is prohibitive for twice per week for at least 8 weeks. 

Both Spravato doses were superior to placebo by approximately 24 hours and remained superior at four weeks.

Published analyses of this study found remission in approximately 22â23% of Spravato-treated patients versus roughly 8% with placebo. That translates to an approximate number needed to treat of 7 for one additional remission.
Spravato can rapidly improve the depressive syndrome in suicidal patients, but it is not proven to make an actively suicidal patient safe.

Adverse effects

Common or clinically important effects include:

sedation in 48â61% by formal rating scales;
dissociative/perceptual symptoms in roughly 61â84%, depending on population and dose;
nausea in 27â32%;
vomiting in 6â12%;
transient systolic blood-pressure elevation averaging approximately 7â10 mmHg above placebo around 40 minutes;
loss of consciousness in approximately 0.3â0.4%.

Patients must receive it in a REMS-certified setting, remain monitored for at least two hours and not drive until the next day after restful sleep.

Evidence for IV ketamine is actually quite strong in refractory depression, though less standardized than FDA-approved esketamine. Ketamine is not FDA-approved for depression, is generic so it discourages commercialization, must be given IV.

Auvelity: The first and only FDA-approved oral NMDA receptor antagonist for MDD. It combines dextromethorphan (an NMDA receptor antagonist) with bupropion (an antidepressant that helps increase the availability of the dextromethorphan).  This is another novel pathway that is being explored by researchers, beyond the traditional serotonin-norepi-dopa axis!  

TMS — noninvasive brain stimulation

Transcranial magnetic stimulation uses magnetic pulses over dorsolateral prefrontal cortex.
Features: outpatient, no anesthesia, no systemic drug exposure,
minimal cognitive side effects; requires daily sessions lasting about 1 hour 5 days/week for 12 weeks or longer;

Eye Movement Desensitization and Reprocessing (EMDR) involve office therapy accompanied by either bilateral visual (with moving LED lights) or auditory stimulation in the context of visualizing prior trauma (quite different than traditional cognitive behavioral talk therapy;
EMDR is supported by over 30 RCTs and is recommended as a first-line PTSD treatment by the WHO, NICE, APA, and ISTSS. 
For adults with childhood trauma-related PTSD (Ch-PTSD) specifically:
The IREM trial (n=155) demonstrated that EMDR produced large effect sizes (d=1.73) in reducing PTSD symptoms from childhood trauma, with a notably low dropout rate of 7.7%. EMDR also reduced depression, dissociation, and trauma-related cognitions. 

COMP360 is one of the most interesting developments in psychiatry in decades. Unlike traditional antidepressants that are taken daily for months or years, COMP360 is a pharmaceutical-grade synthetic psilocybin administered in a highly structured clinical setting, usually as a single dosing session with psychological support before, during, and after treatment.

Where does it stand with the FDA?

The situation has changed rapidly.

Compass Pathways recently reported that both Phase 3 trials met their primary endpoints in treatment-resistant depression (TRD), which is depression that has failed at least two prior antidepressant treatments. The FDA has granted a rolling NDA review process, bringing the drug closer to approval.

Many analysts now view COMP360 as one of the most likely psychedelic medicines to receive FDA approval, potentially in late 2026 or 2027 depending on the final review timeline.

What exactly is the treatment?

A typical COMP360 treatment involves:

Screening and psychiatric evaluation
Several preparatory psychotherapy sessions
One supervised psilocybin session (typically 25 mg)
Several "integration" sessions afterward

The psychedelic experience lasts approximately 6â8 hours, during which the patient is monitored by trained therapists.

This is very different from simply taking "magic mushrooms" recreationally.

How effective is it?

The most impressive aspect is the speed of response.

Traditional SSRIs often require 4â8 weeks for full benefit. COMP360 has demonstrated antidepressant effects beginning as early as the day after treatment in some patients. Several studies have shown clinically meaningful reductions in depression scores after a single administration.

Longer-term follow-up studies suggest some patients maintain benefit for many months after one treatment.

What are the concerns?

As a physician, I recognize that efficacy is only part of the story.

Potential issues include:

Acute anxiety or panic during the psychedelic experience
Temporary increases in blood pressure and heart rate
Risk of precipitating psychosis in vulnerable individuals
Need for specialized monitoring facilities and trained therapists
Cost and reimbursement uncertainty

The FDA will likely scrutinize not only the drug itself but also the entire treatment model, since the psychotherapy and monitoring are integral parts of the intervention.

See table below comparing Spravato with Comp360

Additional cutting edge drugs under development include:

BPL-003 (Synthetic 5-MeO-DMT Nasal Spray)Developed by AtaiBeckley and recently acquired by Eli Lilly in a massive $2.8 billion deal, this is an ultra-fast-acting synthetic formulation of mebufotenin (5-MeO-DMT).Target: Treatment-Resistant Depression (TRD).The Advantage: Unlike psilocybin, which requires a 4-to-6-hour clinic stay, BPL-003's intense psychedelic effects wrap up in 15 to 30 minutes.Current Status: Entering Phase 3 clinical trials, with patients only requiring observation for about two hours post-dose.2. 

Luvesilocin (Psilocin-based Treatment)Luvesilocin is a targeted, newly named psychedelic compound that functions identically to psilocin—the active psychoactive metabolite that the body creates when it processes magic mushrooms.Target: Postpartum Depression (PPD).The Advantage: In an FDA Phase 2 study published by researchers at the University of Colorado, a massive 71% of postpartum women achieved full symptom remission just seven days after a single 30mg dose. It also shows exceptionally low transmission into breast milk, making it highly safe for lactating mothers.Current Status: Moving directly into Phase 3 trials.

Other newer developments involve pharmacogenomics or prediction of clinical response to antidepressant class:

GeneSight is not “FDA approved” in the way a drug is FDA approved. It is a laboratory-developed pharmacogenomic test used to inform prescribing. The FDA has warned broadly that many PGx tests for psychiatric medication response have made claims not reviewed by FDA, especially claims that a test can predict antidepressant effectiveness.

The evidence is mixed, not useless. The large VA PRIME Care randomized trial found PGx-guided care reduced prescribing of medications with predicted drug-gene interactions and produced a small, nonpersistent improvement in remission over 24 weeks. A 2024 American Journal of Psychiatry review concluded that current combinatorial PGx tools are not supported for routine antidepressant selection in major depression.

Where GeneSight may help:

Multiple prior antidepressant failures.
Troublesome side effects.
Concern about CYP2D6/CYP2C19 metabolism.
Choosing among SSRIs/SNRIs/TCAs when several are reasonable.
Increasing patient willingness to try medication because it feels more personalized.

Insurance coverage is challenging (will require documentation) and out-of-pocket costs maybe $300.

Biological theories evolving beyond serotonin
A major intellectual shift is occurring.

The older “chemical imbalance” serotonin narrative is now considered oversimplified.

Modern depression models involve:

stress circuitry dysregulation
inflammation
impaired neuroplasticity
glutamate dysfunction
nmda receptor mediated
reward-network abnormalities
trauma-related network changes
circadian dysfunction

This helps explain why:

SSRIs help some people substantially
others fail multiple serotonergic drugs entirely
rapid-acting glutamatergic agents can work despite bypassing serotonin

Suicidality and rapid intervention: One of the most clinically important developments is recognition that:

suicidal crises can evolve rapidly
waiting 6â8 weeks for medication response is often inadequate

That is why:

ketamine/esketamine
TMS, ECT
intensive outpatient programs
crisis stabilization
psychotherapy focused on safety and emotional regulation have become increasingly emphasized in high-risk depression.

An outstanding recent book that discusses emerging therapies for depression is "Brain Reboot" by Michael Henry, MD (Director of Bipolar Clinic, Mass General, 2022).  This book gives a balanced perspective by an experienced clinician psychiatrist, encompassing cognitive therapy, lifestyle changes, AND pharmacotherapy with emphasis on resistant depression. The target audience is patients, families, and providers.

minimal cognitive side effects; requires daily sessions lasting about 1 hour 5 days/week for 12 weeks or longer;

Eye Movement Desensitization and Reprocessing (EMDR) involve office therapy accompanied by either bilateral visual (with moving LED lights) or auditory stimulation in the context of visualizing prior trauma (quite different than traditional cognitive behavioral talk therapy;
EMDR is supported by over 30 RCTs and is recommended as a first-line PTSD treatment by the WHO, NICE, APA, and ISTSS. 
For adults with childhood trauma-related PTSD (Ch-PTSD) specifically:
The IREM trial (n=155) demonstrated that EMDR produced large effect sizes (d=1.73) in reducing PTSD symptoms from childhood trauma, with a notably low dropout rate of 7.7%. EMDR also reduced depression, dissociation, and trauma-related cognitions. 

COMP360 is one of the most interesting developments in psychiatry in decades. Unlike traditional antidepressants that are taken daily for months or years, COMP360 is a pharmaceutical-grade synthetic psilocybin administered in a highly structured clinical setting, usually as a single dosing session with psychological support before, during, and after treatment.

Where does it stand with the FDA?

The situation has changed rapidly.

Compass Pathways recently reported that both Phase 3 trials met their primary endpoints in treatment-resistant depression (TRD), which is depression that has failed at least two prior antidepressant treatments. The FDA has granted a rolling NDA review process, bringing the drug closer to approval.

Many analysts now view COMP360 as one of the most likely psychedelic medicines to receive FDA approval, potentially in late 2026 or 2027 depending on the final review timeline.

What exactly is the treatment?

A typical COMP360 treatment involves:

Screening and psychiatric evaluation
Several preparatory psychotherapy sessions
One supervised psilocybin session (typically 25 mg)
Several "integration" sessions afterward

The psychedelic experience lasts approximately 6â8 hours, during which the patient is monitored by trained therapists.

This is very different from simply taking "magic mushrooms" recreationally.

How effective is it?

The most impressive aspect is the speed of response.

Traditional SSRIs often require 4â8 weeks for full benefit. COMP360 has demonstrated antidepressant effects beginning as early as the day after treatment in some patients. Several studies have shown clinically meaningful reductions in depression scores after a single administration.

Longer-term follow-up studies suggest some patients maintain benefit for many months after one treatment.

What are the concerns?

As a physician, I recognize that efficacy is only part of the story.

Potential issues include:

Acute anxiety or panic during the psychedelic experience
Temporary increases in blood pressure and heart rate
Risk of precipitating psychosis in vulnerable individuals
Need for specialized monitoring facilities and trained therapists
Cost and reimbursement uncertainty

The FDA will likely scrutinize not only the drug itself but also the entire treatment model, since the psychotherapy and monitoring are integral parts of the intervention.

See table below comparing Spravato with Comp360

Additional cutting edge drugs under development include:

BPL-003 (Synthetic 5-MeO-DMT Nasal Spray)Developed by AtaiBeckley and recently acquired by Eli Lilly in a massive $2.8 billion deal, this is an ultra-fast-acting synthetic formulation of mebufotenin (5-MeO-DMT).Target: Treatment-Resistant Depression (TRD).The Advantage: Unlike psilocybin, which requires a 4-to-6-hour clinic stay, BPL-003's intense psychedelic effects wrap up in 15 to 30 minutes.Current Status: Entering Phase 3 clinical trials, with patients only requiring observation for about two hours post-dose.2. 

Luvesilocin (Psilocin-based Treatment)Luvesilocin is a targeted, newly named psychedelic compound that functions identically to psilocin—the active psychoactive metabolite that the body creates when it processes magic mushrooms.Target: Postpartum Depression (PPD).The Advantage: In an FDA Phase 2 study published by researchers at the University of Colorado, a massive 71% of postpartum women achieved full symptom remission just seven days after a single 30mg dose. It also shows exceptionally low transmission into breast milk, making it highly safe for lactating mothers.Current Status: Moving directly into Phase 3 trials.

Other newer developments involve pharmacogenomics or prediction of clinical response to antidepressant class:

GeneSight is not “FDA approved” in the way a drug is FDA approved. It is a laboratory-developed pharmacogenomic test used to inform prescribing. The FDA has warned broadly that many PGx tests for psychiatric medication response have made claims not reviewed by FDA, especially claims that a test can predict antidepressant effectiveness.

The evidence is mixed, not useless. The large VA PRIME Care randomized trial found PGx-guided care reduced prescribing of medications with predicted drug-gene interactions and produced a small, nonpersistent improvement in remission over 24 weeks. A 2024 American Journal of Psychiatry review concluded that current combinatorial PGx tools are not supported for routine antidepressant selection in major depression.

Where GeneSight may help:

Multiple prior antidepressant failures.
Troublesome side effects.
Concern about CYP2D6/CYP2C19 metabolism.
Choosing among SSRIs/SNRIs/TCAs when several are reasonable.
Increasing patient willingness to try medication because it feels more personalized.

Insurance coverage is challenging (will require documentation) and out-of-pocket costs maybe $300.

Biological theories evolving beyond serotonin
A major intellectual shift is occurring.

The older “chemical imbalance” serotonin narrative is now considered oversimplified.

Modern depression models involve:

stress circuitry dysregulation
inflammation
impaired neuroplasticity
glutamate dysfunction
nmda receptor mediated
reward-network abnormalities
trauma-related network changes
circadian dysfunction

This helps explain why:

SSRIs help some people substantially
others fail multiple serotonergic drugs entirely
rapid-acting glutamatergic agents can work despite bypassing serotonin

Suicidality and rapid intervention: One of the most clinically important developments is recognition that:

suicidal crises can evolve rapidly
waiting 6â8 weeks for medication response is often inadequate

That is why:

ketamine/esketamine
TMS, ECT
intensive outpatient programs
crisis stabilization
psychotherapy focused on safety and emotional regulation have become increasingly emphasized in high-risk depression.

An outstanding recent book that discusses emerging therapies for depression is "Brain Reboot" by Michael Henry, MD (Director of Bipolar Clinic, Mass General, 2022).  This book gives a balanced perspective by an experienced clinician psychiatrist, encompassing cognitive therapy, lifestyle changes, AND pharmacotherapy with emphasis on resistant depression. The target audience is patients, families, and providers.

text: Let me reinforce this article.My experience with AI engines, as a physician and as a patient, is spectacular! I tried them all and cannot really advocate one more than another. I use ChatGPT more so and I think it is more "human" in its tone and acts more as a coach (sycophantic?).Open Evidence is what physicians use in practice for AI guidance from the medical literature. That is great for that function. However, as a patient, I am looking for more than just facts. Surprisingly, the interpretation and contextualization of these facts is remarkable and on point. I have uploaded x-ray images, EKGs, 72-hour cardiac Holter data, variety of lab results from friends and family. I have posed some serious and impactful mental health-type questions. Uniformly, I am blown away by the correctness, the caveats suggested, the alternatives, and the tone of responses. It has shined particularly well in mental health scenarios, as to appropriate words to use in tense situations.  It is true that I am not just a casual or lay user.I am aware of high-profile case reports where AI "hallucinates" or where AI didn't warn adequately about suicidal states.  The systems are becoming incrementally better in front of our eyes. The issue is NOT whether they should replace healthcare provides. No one should suggest that. But they are an additive tool for education, fairly accurate information that patients could use in preparation for discussion with providers. On the other hand, providers should become quite familiar and literal with these tools and not glibly dismiss them or be threatened by them. There will be creative experimentation to find niche roles. These tools are here to stay, and we all need to adapt and understand their utility!

text:
I am quite concerned this Easter weekend about Trump’s tweets and apparent escalation from his news conference few days ago (he has scheduled a Mon 1p news conference with reporters) and hinted at a shock and awe on Tuesday.

POTUS Sun AM: “Open the Fuckin’ Strait, you crazy bastards, or you’ll be living in Hell — JUST WATCH. Praise be to Allah.”

This rhetoric and threats to civilian infrastructure (war crimes per many treaties) will have unintended consequences to the moderate Iranian public, who have endured a repressive regime, to rally against this effort at regime change.

Why didn't Iran develop a nuclear weapon or shut down the Straits in over 47 years? despite sanctions, isolation, etc. Until now.  Reporting suggests that the June 2025, 12-day bombing, left Iran weakened, emboldening Netanyahu (and Trump) to seize the moment to attempt the current war to find a "permanent" solution.

We are in a bad place now with no obvious off-ramp. The Iranian hardliners under military control have a strong incentive to complete development and test a nuclear device for survival and deterrence, similar to N. Korea and Pakistan (and Israel). This is NOT a good thing for the world. But the current “incentive structure” favors this outcome. Hormuz Straits and oil dependency is a choke hold that I do not see a way around a determined and cornered Iran. 

It is interesting that the prior Ayatollah had a fatwah against nuclear weapons. 

Yes—but it’s more complicated than it sounds.

Ali Khamenei (Iran’s last supreme leader) repeatedly stated that nuclear weapons are forbidden under Islam, issuing what is commonly referred to as a fatwa (religious ruling).
 â¢ As early as the mid-1990s, and publicly around 2003â2005, he declared that:
 â¢ Producing, stockpiling, and using nuclear weapons is prohibited
 â¢ He later reinforced this, calling nuclear weapons “haram” (religiously forbidden)  

Iranian officials frequently cited this ruling as a key reason the country did not pursue nuclear weapons.

But there are major caveats

Experts and analysts disagree on how solid or binding that prohibition really was:
 1. Ambiguity about the fatwa itself
 â¢ Some argue it was never issued as a single formal written decree, but rather inferred from speeches and statements  
 2. It may not be permanent
 â¢ In Islamic jurisprudence, a fatwa can be changed by the same authority if circumstances change  
 3. Interpretation has varied
 â¢ At times, Khamenei seemed to forbid all aspects (development, stockpiling, use)
 â¢ At other times, statements suggested opposition mainly to use, not necessarily development  
 4. Even Iranian officials hinted it could change
 â¢ Some suggested Iran might reconsider if under extreme threat (“cornered”)  

After his death (2026 context)
 â¢ The fatwa was personal to Khamenei, not a binding state law
 â¢ With his death, its authority is uncertain or possibly gone, depending on the new leadership  

Bottom line
 â¢ Yes: The last ayatollah did publicly forbid nuclear weapons on religious grounds.
 â¢ However:
 â¢ The ruling was not universally accepted as fixed or binding policy
 â¢ It was potentially reversible
 â¢ And its practical impact on Iran’s nuclear strategy remains debated

text:
I am not really a partisan hack, but I am more interested and aware than in prior midterms (for obvious reasons).  

Here is a distillation of various races (US house, senate, and gubernatorial).  This is of course quite dynamic and subject to change but is a useful reference list to get you aware and started!

As of March 29, 2026, the broad picture is this: Republicans still hold both chambers, but the House looks more exposed than the Senate. The current House breakdown is 217 Republicans, 214 Democrats, 1 independent, and 3 vacancies; with all 435 seats filled, 218 is the majority, so Democrats need a net gain of 4 seats for a clear outright House majority. In the Senate, Republicans hold a 53-47 edge when counting the two independents who caucus with Democrats, so Democrats need a net gain of 4 seats there as well.  ï¿¼

Bottom line: if I had to rank the three arenas by likelihood of a power shift, I would put them in this order: House first, governorships second, Senate third. That is partly structural: the president’s party usually loses House ground in midterms, and Sabato notes exactly that historical pattern for 2026. Cook’s House ratings also show many more vulnerable Republican-held seats than Democratic-held ones at the top of the battlefield.  ï¿¼

House of Representatives

The House is the clearest national battlefield. Cook rates 17 seats as Toss-up, and 13 of those are Republican-held versus 4 Democratic-held. That asymmetry gives Democrats a cleaner path to a takeover than Republicans have to expanding their edge. Reuters likewise describes the GOP as defending a narrow majority while Democrats try to win enough seats to control the chamber.  ï¿¼

title: This is a good podcast to understand the dynamic of the Iranian history and potential history of…
text:
This is a good podcast to understand the dynamic of the Iranian history and potential history of their animosity towards the US and Israel based on events over the past 50-75 years. The interview is with an Iranian scholar who is not an apologist for the regime but someone who translates the recent history. The majority of the Iranian population are moderate and aspire for a better economic lot for themselves and are educated and western leaning. However, they are stuck in a theocracy that is aging and they want to turn the page. The policies taken by the west has been shortsighted and counterproductive.  

JCPOA, negotiated with Iran in 2015 (includes US, Iran, UK, France, China, Russia, Germany), was a vehicle to moderate and negotiate in good faith and with IAEA monitoring (was not perfect, as most such contentious efforts are). That was ripped up in 2018 (day 1 after election by Trump). Since then, it has been bellicosity and saber rattling, and now a hot war, with zero prospects of any trust in the near future (and certainly no chance or the US to be the peacemaker or to take a high road and leave it to Pakistan).

The current war is simply going to give a new generation of hardliners to dig in and invoke religious basis! The western policies are largely punishing the large middle class, the group that should be the basis for moderation and change. 

The current conflict, with impact on oil, only invites the likes of Russia and China to play a role in a way that will complicate the US agenda.  The bellicose messaging by the administration is shortsighted and might appeal to a narrow domestic audience but alienate the Iranian middle class.
